title: Finding Your Middle Way
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: The talk explores the tension between intense spiritual practices and accessibility, suggesting that there may be value in balancing both approaches without problematic elements like misogyny and guru worship. Nomon Tim Burnett notes that exploring this balance requires trust, patience, curiosity, and openness, encouraging the community to consider their own experiences and needs in finding a path that works for them. This approach can help navigate the complexities of spiritual practice, avoiding harm while still offering profound insights and healing.

sentences.text: On the screen we have Scott and Ariel.
Good to see you both.
I think Neil was there earlier, maybe.
There's a good little batch of bodhisattvas here.
Somehow they all got themselves down here.
It takes a little effort, doesn't it?
I doubt that many of us at 6:45 or when we had to leave were like, "Yippee, I've got so much energy, I'm so excited, I can't wait to get out."
But we got here.
Maybe you felt that way, that's wonderful.
I've been talking to people more lately about what the program should be, a kind of preparation for the new building.
There's a survey, and people email me and call me and stuff.
One of the things that was interesting and made sense to me was that there's a lot of diversity.
Naturally there are several things where it could be this or it could be that.
About half the people I hear from want this and the other half want that.
That's just how it goes.
One of those is not exactly about the schedule, but about how we do things.

I've gotten a fair amount of feedback in the last months, year, or two maybe, about how wonderful it is if the talk isn't too long and there's time for discussion, maybe small groups, where you can really talk.
So I've been trying to do that.
Then I also got the feedback, "I hesitate to go because there's too much talking.
So loud and busy."
A person speaking identifies as an introvert and would like to be able to just be quiet.
That's beautiful, both are beautiful, aren't they?
To connect through language from the heart, especially when we have some settledness around it, like in a small group, it's beautiful.
To be able to come here and practice and be glad to be here and interact with everyone completely silently and not say a word, that's beautiful too.
So I thought maybe in terms of small group discussion times, more or less every other time.
Anyway, I was thinking this would be a long talk, but then we'll see what happens.
I don't really know what's going to happen.
I think I would know.
But isn't that interesting?
Different strokes for different folks, as the song goes.
So I want to explore something a little bit tonight that I think about a lot.
I have trouble quite balancing it in my mind or quite saying it right.
It's an area people can have strong opinions about also.

It's the beginning of a conversation, or a continuing conversation, as a community around whether the practice emphasizes intensity, intense, clear, you could say hard sometimes practice, or the practice emphasizes accessibility, flexibility, adaptability, individual modifications and so on.
Both feel important.
And they seem at first to be a little bit like opposites.
There's the strict kind of practice and the relaxed kind of practice.
Is there a middle ground?
Is it sometimes one, sometimes the other, for any given person or any given community?
Part of what's going on, I think, is that we're part of a trajectory, and then a kind of reaction to that trajectory, as American Zen Center.
American Zen started out pretty strongly on the intense side of the spectrum when it was brought to the Euro-American mainstream culture anyway.
Of course, Buddhism had been brought to immigrant communities 50 years, 100 years before people like Suzuki Roshi, Chogyam Trungpa and others showed up in the 50s and 60s.

But somehow when this second wave that led most directly to what we're doing happened in the 50s and 60s, I don't know that someone like Suzuki Roshi thought, "This needs to be really intense and sort of harsh."
I think he was just doing what he always did.
And he had apparently definitely some strength in practice, but also a lot of sweetness.

But it seems like what happened is that the students receiving these Asian teachers, who were mostly men, the teachers were pretty much all men, really got hooked on a kind of vision or idea of breakthrough experience, enlightenment writ large.
And it just seemed natural that the way to get that, because it would be really hard to get, would be to work really hard and to practice really hard in a very intense environment.
So there's a big emphasis on pushing, trying, doing it really well, not moving, being full on at all times, so that this would lead to the outcome that this all seemed to be about.

One ingredient there was projections on the teacher, which certainly would have affected the teachers themselves: that the Roshi or the Rinpoche, the guru, by definition already has that, whatever that is, and has clear insight into everything and everybody, and is always right in everything they do or say.
Even if they do something weird or apparently unethical, that is still a manifestation of enlightenment, but we just don't understand why yet.
We don't get it yet.

In our particular lineage, as far as we know, Suzuki Roshi kept the precepts and was ethical, but as you know, there are many stories of teachers who didn't so much, including to some extent Suzuki Roshi's successor, Richard Baker, and he also received that projection that he himself had given to Suzuki Roshi.
And that stuff changes you.
So the whole thing started out kind of that way in America.

Then after this long series of scandals, and some people being seriously harmed for sure, some less so, there was a lot of soul searching and institutional changes and therapy and reparations, and the practice gradually softened, for some probably not quickly enough, for others probably disturbingly quickly.
And now the main practice, Buddhist practice in convert sanghas like ours, is gentler, more caring, more inclusive.
It has a bit of a clue about being trauma sensitive.

It tries to think about and understand the power dynamics involved, and how systemic injustices, such as around gender, race, sexual orientation and identification, aren't just out there in the bad old world, they're in here as well.
There's plenty further to go in that journey, that's for sure.
But that's part of what happened and it's a good thing, which I really agree with.
I and all of us, I'm sure, have a lot more to learn on this journey toward a Dharma that's responsive, loving, connected and compassionate.
But then the question comes up for me: does anything get lost?
Does anything important get lost in that process, that journey of making things safer, gentler and more inclusive?
Are there actually some benefits to intensity in practice, to difficult practices, to sustaining practices, even when they challenge us in a lot of ways?
The challenge in all of this is that it's so hard to know.
We all have our subjective opinions, but our ability to evaluate what's going on for us and what's going on in practice is shaky at best.
Stuff's happening so much more below the surface than our conscious awareness even understands.
It requires a lot of trust, I think, and a lot of patience and a lot of curiosity and a lot of openness to explore this.
What's our way?
What's the most helpful way?
Is it just one way?
Is it a broad array of ways?
I've been thinking about this for ages, and sometimes I don't express it as well or as clearly as I could, and maybe it comes out a little judgy sometimes.
But I think we in some ways need both of these paths, without the misogyny and guru worship.
We'll just toss that in the garbage.
But there is something there that's valuable.
So it was really fascinating to go to Japan and see both plenty of gentleness and kindness and also to learn about some very intense ways of practice, very intense.
On the whole, Japanese culture appears, at least to us visitors and the people we met anyway, extremely kind and polite, respectful and considerate, almost to an extreme degree.
One example of zillions: Razal and I took a little airporter bus to the airport.
The driver got out before anybody, bowed to every person and thanked them for riding the bus.
Every person.
And at the same time, you're like, "I'm nobody."
And also within that culture there are lots of forms of Buddhism, and there's a lot of overlap between them too.
I have constellated some very intense, hard practices, and we met some practitioners who experienced this and practiced in that way.
The interesting thing was that, at least the folks we met came out the other side embodying kindness, humility, warmth.
They seemed pretty clear and insightful too.
Just really humble.
You could easily imagine somebody who did a really, really unimaginably hard practice would come out a little chuffed with themselves, right?
They'd come out ready for everyone to be impressed by them.
Probably they should be given a high position of authority and a lot of nice stuff or something, but that wasn't the case.
It's a pretty small sample size, just thinking of a couple of people, but people who did really intense practices.
It really got me thinking about this again.
What's the value of intense practice?
How can it be done in a way that's healthy?
Is there something lost if we're a little too quick to gentle practice?
I don't have an answer to that, but I want to tell you about one of the people we met.
This was one of our favorite days on the trip.
We met a 48-year-old monk named Mitsunaga Endo, who is now not known by his name.
Nobody actually called him by that name, but he's known by a title, which is Dai Ajari, because he completed one of the hardest imaginable practices that I've ever heard of.
This is the deep practice called Kaiho-gyo, which in English is often referred to as the Marathon Monk practice.
It's a practice done on a particular sacred mountain that we got to visit called Mount Hiei.
It's just above Kyoto to the northeast.
His title is pretty intense, actually.
Maybe he's used to being called this, but Dai Ajari: Dai means great, and Ajari is the Japanese voicing of Arhat.
And an Arhat is an awakened one.
So to us it just sounds like sounds, Dai Ajari, Dai Ajari, Dai Ajari.
But imagine everyone who meets you says, "Hello, great awakened one."
And then there are also honorifics that get added to the ends of names.
The normal respectful one is San, and a rare one only used for emperors and really important people is Sama.
So people use that with him as well.
So it's Dai Ajari Sama.
So, hello, great awakened one that everyone is completely impressed and amazed by.
So let me tell you about his practice.
The Buddhism that he's a part of is Tendai Buddhism.
Tendai Buddhism has a really broad range of practices and sub-sects who emphasize different practices.
They study a lot of different texts.
They're fans of the Lotus Sutra.
So if you've done Lotus Sutra studies yet, here's another group of Lotus Sutra fans.
They're all over the place actually.

Tendai Buddhism dominated Buddhism in Japan from about the year 800 to the 1300s and into the 1400s, and then it lost its dominance when Zen and Pure Land schools took over and divided up the pie of Japanese Buddhism.
So they reduced down mostly to their sacred mountain.
We live by really big mountains.
This is like a 2800-foot-tall mountain, a small mountain, but it's its own little mountain, and they have the whole place.
It's their mountain.
This particular sect that this fellow is a part of, the Marathon Monk sect, the Kai Ho Gyo sect, they think started soon after this whole school started in the 800s.
And just in case you're curious, Tendai is also a transplanted version of a Chinese school.
Just like Dogen went to China, the founder of Tendai Buddhism, named Sai Cho, went to China.
He was really impressed by his teachers and the school of Buddhism he found there that was called Tien Tai in Chinese, and he brought a version of it back to Japan where it did transform.
Here's the blurb about Tendai Buddhism from the Wikipedia page.
*A key part of Tendai Buddhism's teaching is that enlightenment can be attained in the current life and it's through the process of selfless service and devotion that this can be achieved.
The Tendai Buddhists practice selfless service and devotion in many ways, but the Kai Ho Gyo is seen as the ultimate expression of this commitment.*
So the core of their practice is 100-day stretches, 100 days in a row, no days off.
The Kai Ho Gyo practitioner, called a Gyoja, gets up about 2 in the morning and puts on a special dress that's particular to this tradition.
He wears white robes and straw sandals, carries a staff and an oil lamp, and wears a very special hat.
It's a really interesting looking little hat.
I'll put some pictures on the website.
I actually didn't organize a show tonight, sorry.
And the white robe is really significant.
Usually people don't wear white in Japan.
White is the color of death.
So we wear black robes.
So that's already pretty weird and extreme, to wear white robes.
To us it's just a color, I guess, but I think it's a big deal.
Anyway, the person gets up at 2 in the morning, puts all this on, and then runs for 25 miles.
It's a smooth, fast trot.
They keep their upper body really still and they trot along with their staff and their oil lamp, because it's dark.
They do not wear a headlamp.
This is an ancient tradition.
And this 25-mile run sounds really impressive to us, but actually it's not the important part of their practice.
The important part is they stop, sometimes very briefly, sometimes a little longer, at about 260 little trailside shrines every night.
In every one there are different mudras to do and chants to offer and prayers to say.
And they do a lot of stuff with their mala beads or juzu beads that is ritualized and specific as well.
Each of the 260 stops has a little different ritual.
We asked him, what are the rituals, and he said, sorry, it's secret.
So you have to actually do this practice to learn them.
As far as I know, no non-Japanese person has attempted it.

All this needs to be finished by the time the monks wake up back home at the temple and get up to do their regular practice of morning service, meditation, meals, cleaning, chores, taking care of the temple like a monk does.
The person doing this kaihokyo, marathon practice, is expected to participate just as normal with all that too.
So it's an unbelievably long day.
And then you do it again, and again, and again, and again.
This is done for 100 days in a row, the first year.
Then I guess they probably go more or less back to their usual daily practice, which is already pretty strenuous.
And they do it again the next year and the next year, and the whole thing takes seven years.
In the end, they will have done this practice a thousand times, a thousand times, over seven years.
An interesting side note, I just learned this today, I'm very excited: part of the origin story of kaihokyo is the story in the Lotus Sutra of the Bodhisattva Never Disparaging.
Yeah.
So that's the attitude they're supposed to bring to this.
Bodhisattva Never Disparaging had a unique practice.
He was a very humble monk who committed himself to loving and caring for everybody and not giving up on anyone ever, and not offending anybody, not causing any harm whatsoever.
So eventually he figured out the only thing he could safely do was to bow to people and say one thing.
The way it's translated from the Chinese, he doesn't sound great in English, but everyone he ran into would say, I have profound reverence for you, I would never treat you with disparagement.
And in the Lotus Sutra, people did treat him right back with disparagement.
Ah, you dope, you know, threw stuff at him, maybe threw banana peels.
Anyway, that spirit of reverence for everyone is what the kaihokyo practitioner should bring to all their encounters with other humans, but also with all these spirits of the mountain.
It's a very spiritual thing.
I've mentioned this before, but you may have gotten into Zen because you thought it was very rational and there's no gods and spirits.
No.
There are many, many gods and spirits.
There's not one overarching guy with a big beard or anything like that, but there are many.

I don't know if they would even say the word gods, it's hard to translate across languages and cultures, but many mythosymbolic beings, probably actually real in a certain way, are involved in Japanese Buddhism.
One of the important ones is this really fierce-looking guy named Fudo Myo-O, important to these guys.
He's got a big skull and these really intense eyes and a sword, and his other hand is in a fist.
Sometimes he has stuff in that hand.
He's so intense that flames naturally erupt from the back of his head.
And he's not a violent character, he's a fierce character, and his job is to protect the Dharma.
Nobody's messing with this Dharma.
He protects the practitioners and protects the world.
So he's kind of like the patron saint of this practice.
This intense practice has an intense Bodhisattva figure called Fudo Myo-O.
So let me tell you about the rest of the practice.
The first three years you do the hundred marathons of about 25 miles.
In years four and five you up it to 200 days in a row instead of 100.
In year six the route extends from 25 miles to about 35 miles, so you've got to get up earlier to get it done in time for the morning.
And then in the seventh year the route leaves the mountain and descends down to the city of Kyoto, to include shrines and the people of the city.
The home leavers return to the home dwellers.
When we heard about this, the Daiajari mentioned it was a recent addition to the routine, which turned out to mean like late 1800s or something.
That was recent.
So it's just a different frame of time here as well.
Since this practice was established sometime in the late 800s, it's been completed by 51 people, and this was the 50th person, the one we were talking to and spending the day with.
Anyway, when he includes Kyoto for the last year, he's going 50 miles a day.
He's also navigating with the help of a group of lay supporters.
They help him out, going through a modern busy city doing this ancient ritual in straw sandals and white robes and staff and a special hat.
He has to stop at stoplights and stuff.
He and the ladies who helped organize this were English speakers, so they could translate for him.
Poor Ray, who was doing great with her Japanese, was at sea with him.
He had a weird accent so she couldn't understand him, and some strange expressions.
I think it was actually kind of frustrating, because she was trying to figure out her Japanese and then it was hard for her to hear the English.
And they were repeating it.
Anyway, it was sweet.
She did a great job, Ray.
It was wonderful.
She took care of her things really well and navigated the culture with us.
But anyway, as he's going through Kyoto each day for 100 days, gradually it becomes known this is happening.
The crowds start lining up.
Then the crowds start snarling traffic and causing secondary problems.
Then the police are involved.
It becomes this whole big thing.
He does this every night.
Well, I guess it would be morning.
It would be daylight by the time you get down to Kyoto.
So I think for that last year they tell him, okay, you don't have to sweep the courtyard anymore, we'll let you sleep.
I think.
He didn't say that, but I assume so.
How can you do 50 miles and get back in time to open the temple?
But here's the really intense part.
That was the warm up.
During the fifth year he does an intense meditation retreat called Do-Iri, which means entering the temple.
Do is temple.
Temple entering.
For this nine-day retreat his whole assignment is to recite the mantra of Fudo Myo-O.
Each different deity or Bodhisattva has their own mantra, so Fudo Myo-O has a mantra you recite.
And that's it for nine days straight.
Nothing else should or can be done.
So no sleeping.
No rest.
No food.
No water.
Two support monks sit by both sides.
I think they probably rotate.
They make sure he doesn't fall over, keep an eye on him and support him.
The only thing that happens once a day is he gets up.
Through each day the support monks have to help him more.
They showed us a picture of him five or six days in, and you can kind of tell he's having trouble walking.
They get up together and walk up this trail a little bit to a very special well which has holy water in it.
His job is to scoop up some water, put it in a bucket and bring it back to Fudo Myo-O as an offering.
As part of that process he can rinse out his mouth with the water, but he may not drink.
The monks are watching him, making sure to help him not stray.
And this is done at 2 a.m.
It's like the whole thing.
It's like, wow.
Can humans imagine a more intense, mystical, life-altering, barely impossible, somehow possible ritual?
It's unbelievable.

A funny thing he said was that actually rinsing his mouth out made things harder, because he got used to no moisture over 23 and a half hours, and then water in his mouth jolted his system and reminded him that he hadn't drunk.
He told us he figures that a human can survive for maybe seven days with that kind of practice, without drinking and eating or resting.
This is nine days long.
So he knows the reason why he's still alive is that Fudo Myo-O helped him.
This fierce character helped him.
And then it was Fudo's energy.
I don't know what word he used exactly: energy, power, love.
But it was Fudo Myo-O that helped him through.
It wasn't self power.
It wasn't his effort.
It wasn't gritting his teeth.
It was letting go into the embrace of this fierce protector.
So we got to have some question and answer, and we were actually sitting inside the hall where he did this meditation retreat.
It was powerful.
We were in the Myoo-do.
One of the first questions somebody asked him was the first thing we would think about, right: did you ever think about giving up?
He kind of shook his head.
I don't remember exactly what he said.
I don't know if any of you guys remember, but he kind of shook his head and said that question doesn't compute.
What?
Giving up?
It just didn't occur to him over seven years.
He had set out to do this.
He was literally doing it one step at a time.
And that was his whole entire life.
Maybe it helped that he grew up in the monastic establishment in some way.
He ordained pretty young.
And apparently his family of origin was, I'm not sure, impoverished or not able to totally take care of him in some way.
It was not clear.
He was more or less adopted by his teacher, and his teacher became kind of his adopted father too.
So this was his family.
And like I was saying, coming out of this, just kind, humble, a little reserved, maybe.
I got to sit across from him at lunch, and there was zero small talk or gestures or even looking at me as far as I could tell, until I finally thought of a question to ask him.
Then he answered.
All this was through the translator, which adds a little layer of awkwardness, so I don't want to read anything into that.
He seemed like a perfectly warm guy.
As we were walking along, we found the new guy.
The next guy was there, weeding the garden or something.
And our Daiajari asked him how it was going and had he had much trouble with leeches.
It sounded like he kind of said, hey, how are the leeches?
They have some kind of ground-borne leeches on this mountain, so that's a problem if you're in straw sandals in the middle of the night.
Maybe that was one of the steps, to get the leeches off.
And then what happened next, apparently, is he just had more responsibilities.
He needs to teach young monks.
I'm sure he would have been welcome to still live in the temple as an ordinary monk, but he was not offered the abbot's position or any new special anything.
What he ended up doing was moving off the mountain and taking over an abandoned temple, gathering support from the local village to help him fix it up, and learning how to grow rice.

All over this part of central Japan, there are still very small rice farmers, which actually, it turns out, is because Japan has enormous tariffs on the enormous rice farms other places, but that's another story.
They keep that tradition alive.
So that's what he's doing, hanging out in the village, running this little temple, growing rice.
He didn't go on a speaking circuit.
He didn't write a book.
He didn't do any workshops.
He's not giving motivational speeches.
He's taking care of his rice and his students and little by little repairing this temple, spending a day with tourists once in a while.
The ladies who organized it said this is only the fourth or fifth time or something they've done this, and most of the other groups have been full of athletes.
You want to just look at them and say, can I see your quads or something?
He doesn't look really pumped or anything.
I mean, he looks fit.
But I think for him, that wasn't the main part at all.
At one point we asked if he still ran.
He said, yeah, a little.
Now it was more about this engagement with the spirits and places of the Sacred Mountain.
It was about the merit and spiritual energy generated by doing this practice.
It was about his being willing to do this to keep this tradition alive.
It was about letting go of his own agenda completely.
So I don't think he expected anything out of it, and he probably knew from the previous ones.
There had been a little cluster of them, only 51 over hundreds of years, and then there've been three or four, maybe five, in the 20th and 21st centuries.
So it's having a bit of a revival, I guess, this practice, which is kind of amazing.
Similarly, last week I was telling you about Tom Kirschner, whom we enjoyed meeting.
Same kind of thing, though not as picture-book amazing as the marathon thing.
He was the American who moved to Kyoto in the 70s because he fell in love with the idea of Eastern culture and Japan, and discovered how much that was informed by Buddhism when he got there.
Then he fell head over heels for Buddhism and ordained as a monk.
He's the only American known, I think, through the complete Rinzai Zen training there, and it sounds like he did it multiple times in multiple places.
He said each place had a different method, so I think he did the whole thing like three times or something.
This was a lot of intense Zen practice, like being on sesshin for us, but a harder sesshin than we do, for 90-day stretches in a row where you do not leave.
You're in the middle of this bustling city, but you do not leave that monastic enclosure.
You get up early, you do a ton of zazen, you work, there's very little rest.
And then the funny part, he says: we finally go to bed, at 10 o'clock or something at night, and we don't really go to bed.
The form is to lie down, spread out our futon and our quilt, which is kept in a little box behind your seat in the meditation hall.
They all live together in the meditation hall.
The lights are turned off, and then we all jump up to go do more meditation outside in the garden.
And he said, "I don't remember any of that meditation in the garden.
I slept through all of it."
But he was so humble.
He didn't say, "It's a weird custom, I don't think they should do that anymore."
He was like, "Yeah, that's just what happened.
Then I snoozed sitting up in the garden."
And this was year-round, including in winter.
They get to wear thicker robes in winter, but the buildings are unheated, and there's no heat.
That was the practice, so that's what he did.
So we're sitting in one of the zendos, one of the monks' halls, sodos, where he trained.
That was a moving moment for me.
We did a period of zazen, and he explained what the daily schedule is for the monks in training, and he shared with us that there aren't that many of them anymore.
I kind of knew this, but it's even more than I knew.
He described all that, and I'll come back to it.
And then he said, "I lived for five years on that seat there."
I was just like, come again?
This was your house?
For five years?
I showed a picture of him to my friend Koshin, who connected us.
I kind of suspected this, but Koshin clarified that when he greeted us at the temple gate, he was wearing beginner monk's robes.
He was wearing novice robes.
The great big belt he was wearing was the belt that the new monks wear.
His rakusu was kind of falling apart, and he was just the sweetest, most humble guy.
They gave him a little place to live at the gatehouse, and he teaches foreign groups like us, he greets foreign groups like ours, and does a little of this and a little of that.
He got married late in life and was enjoying that.
He just loved Zen, he just liked to practice.
But same thing: he could have written a bunch of books about his intense practice and his success.
This includes passing all the koan systems, which are very hard to do.
They're done in cryptic archaic Japanese, and everything has to be memorized in archaic Japanese, so he did an unbelievable thing, actually.
And he could have just been Joe anybody, meeting him.
So it's a fascinating thing to me, to see a couple of examples of intense practice.
You're making me think back to when I started at San Francisco Zen Center in the 1980s.
It was more intense then than it is there now, and certainly more intense there than here, then and now.

I don't remember the full schedule of the first sesshin I sat, for instance, but I think it was something like 4 a.m. wake-up, 9 p.m. bed, a dozen or so 40-minute zazen periods, really long dharma talks, brief breaks, and they asked us not to ever bathe, because that would be too...
I don't know what.
I never quite heard the rationale for that exactly.
No sensory pleasures.
I was 20, almost 21, actually.
And it absolutely was the hardest thing I've ever done in my life.
No question.
Intense physical discomfort, intense anxiety and edginess, and I didn't sleep very well, and the whole thing came to a blur after a while.
I half understood that I was trying too hard.
If you press on your eyeballs from the outside, you can make these little swimmers, this little swimmery image.
I somehow got bug-eyed enough that I could do that by pressing the inside of my eyeballs.
I was seeing these little swimmers all the time.
So I had no idea how tense I was.
Although I did get a little clue when the final bell rang, the final period.
I'd made the enormous strategic mistake of counting up how many periods a day, multiplying by seven, and counting them down.
If you do that, sure enough, when you're at your most miserable, it's going to be a very large number to go.
It's better not to know.
It really is better not to know.
The being-in-the-moment thing is really true, actually.
This is a hard way to learn that, but a powerful way.
Anyway, when that final bell rang, I felt this incredible release.
All this tension fell out, and I was suddenly floating on air.
I was so happy.
Something went from "this is the worst, hardest thing I've ever done" to "this is the best thing I've ever done!
This is amazing!"
And then I decided it was both.
It was the hardest thing ever done and the best thing ever done.
So I don't know.
Did I learn something that I wouldn't have learned if it was a gentler schedule?
Plus, I'd just been a little wiser about it.
I've not pushed myself so very hard.
I don't know.
But I believe I learned something important, because it was hard, because I made it harder.
I guess in a way it doesn't matter what we do.
We'll each make it hard in our own ways.
So I don't know why I'm even worrying about this.
There are plenty of stories of intense practice leading to sudden realizations and some kind of clarity and some kind of big something.
And there are plenty of verified stories of hard practice and intense schedules triggering all kinds of harms.
Psychological harms mostly: people going into psychotic or semi-psychotic states that are hard to get out of after the meditation ends.
